# Wastewater as a critical tool for understanding drug usage


### Biobot is launching a new tool to estimate drug consumption and the number of users within a community


[Josh Harrison](https://substack.com/@harrisonjg)


and[Kait Hess Jimenez, MS](https://substack.com/@kaithessjimenez)


Oct 15, 2026


The nation’s substance use epidemic has touched millions of American homes. Most of us have seen this tragedy firsthand, in our friends, families, or communities. But because of several factors like illegality, stigma, and gaps in care access, the full scope of the epidemic is unknown. For most communities, there simply is not enough data to answer two fundamental questions:


-


How many people are struggling with substance use disorder?


-


How much of a given drug is being consumed?


The need for this information is pressing. It can save lives.


To address these questions, this fall Biobot will release a new feature for customers on our dashboard:


**the Biobot Substance Use Calculator** .


Our calculator will walk public health practitioners through the complex process of estimating drug consumption from wastewater concentrations. We will provide curated options for method of usage, excretion rates, and the other parameters that shape consumption. Don’t worry if these terms are unfamiliar to you! We will provide detailed documentation so you can fully understand how the calculations work.


Importantly, since


**public health practitioners know their communities best** , each parameter in the calculator can easily be changed to fit boots-on-the-ground knowledge. For example, if a public health department knows its community primarily consumes fentanyl by smoking rather than taking pills, that can be specified in the calculator.


The calculator inputs data from our robust analytical chemistry pipeline. Today, Biobot quantifies over 54 substances (with many more to come, stay tuned!), with a turnaround time of five to six business days from sample collection to data delivery. Fentanyl, cocaine, methadone, buprenorphine, and amphetamine will be the first targets that we include in the calculator.


### **How will our calculator work?**


The heart of the calculator is a translation of ‘concentration’ data into ‘consumption’ data. Concentrations tell us how much of a substance is in wastewater; consumption tells us how much of a substance was used.


Once we have an estimate of consumption, we can make inferences regarding the number of people who use drugs in our nation’s communities, the number of doses consumed, and even the street dollar amount associated with those doses.


We will describe our methods in greater detail in subsequent blog posts, but to give you a preview of how the calculations work, let’s think about how a drug ends up in the sewer (Fig. 1).


-


First, a drug must be consumed (smoked, swallowed, snorted, etc.).


-


Second, the drug must be absorbed by the body and metabolized. In this context, ‘metabolized’ means that the body breaks down the substance that was ingested (the parent compound).


-


Third, the metabolites are excreted into the waste stream, thus becoming a component of wastewater.


Fig. 1. The path by which drugs enter wastewater.


Each of these steps is surprisingly hard to estimate. The main difficulty is integrating many studies and figuring out the exact definitions the scientists used during their measurements. For example, an excretion factor could be based on estimating masses of the drug and metabolite excreted, or counting the number of molecules excreted. It could include losses that come from smoking or snorting the drug or exclude them. Even figuring out how much people use per day is extremely challenging, as it is very hard to measure or study. And, of course, all these variables differ among types of drugs: for instance, fentanyl has a different excretion rate than cocaine.


Finally, many parameters are different between regions and over time. For example, the share of smoking for fentanyl nearly doubled in the last four years, and smoking is much more prevalent on the West Coast than elsewhere in the nation.


**We will be staying on top of the scientific literature and updating our recommended parameters as new studies and datasets become available.**


A limitation of the calculator is that we currently assume most compounds are stable in the sewer (except buprenorphine), meaning that our calculations do not account for degradation or unusual chemical interactions that could affect measurement. We are exploring ways to address these limitations.


**We are all in the fight against substance use disorders together. We hope our calculator will give communities the data they need to save lives.**


You can subscribe to our Substack to get future updates delivered straight to your inbox.
